name: Vilvavananathar Temple, Tiruvaikavur
deity: Shiva as Vilvavananathar (Vilvavaneswarar), with the goddess Valaikkai Nayaki (Sarvajana Rakshaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu on the northern bank of the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); Chola-era temple with later additions
summary: Vilvavananathar Temple at Tiruvaikavur, the Lord of the Vilva Forest, is a Tevaram shrine near Kumbakonam, honoured in tradition as the place where the Maha Shivaratri observance began, when a hunter's night in a vilva tree won him release from Yama.

sections.history: Tiruvaikavur, also spoken of as Vaigavur, lies in the Thanjavur district a short way north of Kumbakonam, in the old Chola country on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The temple is praised in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanar saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and tradition places the building in the Chola age. The Lord is called Vilvavananathar, master of the forest of the vilva, the tree whose trifoliate leaves are most dear to Shiva; a local account holds that Shiva himself arose here as a vilva tree in a great deluge. Above all, the village remembers itself as the place where the observance of Maha Shivaratri was first kept.
sections.architecture: A rajagopuram rises over the entrance of this Dravidian temple, and the Shiva linga of Vilvavananathar is worshipped in the sanctum, with the goddess Valaikkai Nayaki honoured as his consort. The temple tank, the Yama Theertham, lies directly across from the main gateway, and tradition holds that Yama himself dug it. A curious feature recalls the temple's legend: the Nandi, the sacred bull, is said to face the entrance gate instead of the sanctum, in the belief that it keeps Yama from coming in. Dakshinamurthy, the Lord as teacher, is described here in an unusual standing posture with a staff.
sections.legends: A hunter once chased a deer into the hermitage of a sage who was worshipping a Shiva linga. The sage refused to hand over the deer, and when the hunter would not give up, he took the form of a tiger to frighten him; in another telling it was Shiva himself who became the tiger. The hunter fled up a nearby tree, which was a vilva, and, to keep himself awake through the night with the tiger waiting below, he plucked its leaves and let them fall. Beneath the tree stood a linga, and the leaves fell upon it. It was the night of Maha Shivaratri, so the hunter had worshipped Shiva all night without knowing it. When Yama came for him the next day, Nandi and Shiva's guardians, with Dakshinamurthy, drove Yama out of the temple. From this the temple is remembered as the origin of Shivaratri, and the tank is called after Yama.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri, kept in the Tamil month of Masi (February to March), is by far the greatest festival of Tiruvaikavur, and is reported to draw vast crowds of devotees, some say as many as two lakh. The celebration runs over two days, closing with the Theerthavari on the new moon day, and a night procession on a palm-leaf cart is part of it. Masi Magam and Panguni Uthiram are also observed, and Vaikasi Visakam, Adipooram and Navaratri are named among the temple's notable occasions. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Tiruvaikavur with the hunter's story in mind. Enter beneath the gateway tower, notice that the Nandi looks outward toward the entrance, and then come to the sanctum of the Lord of the Vilva Forest and to the goddess Valaikkai Nayaki. The Yama Theertham across from the gate is a quiet place to pause, and the temple is remembered as a place of protection from Yama's fear. On ordinary days the village is calm, among the fields near Kumbakonam; on Shivaratri night it fills with devotees keeping vigil, which is the best time to feel what the temple's legend has meant to the countryside for centuries.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days such as Maha Shivaratri.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvaikavur lies in the Kumbakonam area of Thanjavur district, about 17 km by road from Kumbakonam, which is the nearest railway station; Swamimalai is about 7 km away and Thanjavur about 45 km. Buses and local auto-rickshaws serve the village, and a hired car from Kumbakonam is the easiest way to reach it. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport. The nearby Vijayanathar temple at Tiruvijayamangai can be visited on the same day.
